This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU

The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: How I Built a Simple Text Repeater That Runs Fully in the Browser
items.summary: I run a small site of text tools, and the most used one is a text repeater: type a word or emoji once, choose a count, copy the result. Here's how it works and the gotchas I hit. function repeat(text, count, sep) { return Array(count).fill(text).join(sep); } Array(count).fill(text).join(sep) is fast enough for 100,000 copies on a phone. A naive += loop is much slower on large counts. Size limits. 'I love you' 10,000 times on new lines is ~110,000 characters. WhatsApp allows 65,536 per message, so I show a live size (new Blob([out]).size) before the user copies. Emoji. Never reverse or slice strings with split(''); use Array.from(str) or Intl.Segmenter so emoji and Hindi text don't break. Clipboard on mobile. navigator.clipboard.writeText needs a user gesture; keep the copy inside the click handler. Privacy. Everything runs client-side, so nothing is uploaded. The live version is repeat text on RepeatText. If you just want a quick text repeater for WhatsApp or emoji, it's free with no signup. For big jobs there's a repeat text generator that splits long output into parts. Feedback welcome in the comments!

items.summary: When you buy a new mechanical keyboard—or troubleshoot a sticky laptop key—the first thing you usually want to check is whether simultaneous keypresses actually register. Because event.key reflects the active OS keyboard layout and modifier state (for example, Shift + a produces A, and IMEs can emit Process), tracking physical key switches reliably requires event.code. items.title: Why React Needs key: The Bug That Moves Your Input to the Wrong Row
items.summary: Picture a shopping list with a note field on each row: {items.map((item, i) => ( {item.name} ))} The list is Milk, Eggs, Bread. You type "2 dozen" next to Eggs. Then you delete Milk. The list now shows Eggs and Bread, and "2 dozen" sits next to Bread. Nothing crashed, nothing warned. The note moved to the wrong row because of key={i}. Every render, React has to answer one question for each item in the list: "Is this the same item as last time, or a new one?" It answers by looking at the key, like checking name tags at a door. A key is a name tag. React matches items between renders by name tag, not by position. If the tag matches, React keeps that item's state and DOM element and only updates what changed. If a tag disappears, that item is removed. If a new tag shows up, a new item is created. The index makes a bad name tag because it's really a seat number. When someone leaves, everyone behind them moves up a seat, and their tag changes. Comparing the new list to the old one is called reconciliation. items.title: The 7 Threads Running Inside Every Node.js Process
items.summary: Quick Answer: While JavaScript executes strictly on a single thread via the event loop, the Node.js runtime process itself is multi-threaded. An empty Node.js process immediately launches seven OS threads: one main thread for your JavaScript, four V8 engine threads for garbage collection and JIT compilation, one task scheduler thread, and one debug/signal handler. Whenever I hear someone say that Node.js is single-threaded, I understand why they say it. It is one of those industry shorthands we lean on when explaining the event loop, reassuring colleagues that they will not have to wrestle with mutexes, deadlocks, or race conditions when writing application logic. Yet if I fire up an empty Node script in my terminal and inspect the process at the operating system level, I do not see a single thread. I see seven OS threads running immediately. Here is what those threads actually do, and why that distinction matters when you are reasoning about your runtime. An empty Node.js process requires multiple threads because modern runtimes offload background system operations to keep the main execution loop unblocked. items.title: The 3 AM Gateway Leak: Why Your Next.js LLM Integration Needs Server Boundaries
items.summary: The 3 AM Gateway Leak: Why Your Next.js LLM Integration Needs Server Boundaries It is 3 AM. Your on-call alert fires: someone posted your LLM gateway API key to a public GitHub issue. Not because of a breach. Because a developer fixed a missing browser credential by adding NEXT_PUBLIC_ to your .env, and the gateway client landed in a shared module that Client Components could import. The expensive mistake in an AI-enabled Next.js application is rarely model selection. It is treating an authenticated inference request like an ordinary frontend fetch. The failure is architectural, not accidental. A gateway adapter becomes a shared utility. Someone adds a prefix. The application works. And 10,000 lines of minified JavaScript now ship your production secrets to every browser that downloads your app. This is how you avoid that page. The LLM gateway lives on the server side of Next.js. Always. The topology is trivial but unforgiving: Browser → authenticated Server Action → server-only gateway adapter → provider Gateway-side key encryption does not protect credentials accidentally shipped by your application. Upstream failover does not replace application authorization or request budgets.

items.title: Content Moderation API Node.js: A Practical Tutorial
items.summary: Why Add a Content Moderation API to Node.js Apps Node.js powers a large share of the products where user-generated text appears first: chat rooms, comment threads, forums, marketplace listings, community feeds, and support inboxes. In nearly all of those systems the critical moment is the same. A string arrives from a user, and your handler has to decide whether it can be saved, published, or broadcast to everyone else. Adding a content moderation API to a Node.js service is mostly an HTTP integration problem. You send a text to an endpoint, you get JSON back, and you branch on it. There is no model to host, no word list to curate, and no scoring curve to calibrate. CautionLabs keeps that surface small. The hosted API takes a text string and returns two things: A categories object with twelve boolean flags, one per harm category. A single flagged boolean that is true when any category is flagged. That is the whole decision surface. The API is binary by design: it returns no scores, no probabilities, and no confidence values, and there are no thresholds to tune. items.title: How to Debug and Fix Race Conditions in Distributed Node.js Microservices
items.summary: How do you recognize race conditions in asynchronous microservices? Race conditions in distributed Node.js microservices occur when multiple asynchronous operations or independent service instances execute concurrently and attempt to mutate shared state without coordination, leading to data corruption. Recognizing these bugs requires looking for non-deterministic test failures, duplicate processing anomalies, and inventory discrepancies that only appear under high throughput. Because Node.js is single-threaded per event loop, developers often mistakenly assume that async/await syntax provides thread-safe execution blocks. However, across distributed microservices sharing a database or cache, an asynchronous function yields execution control back to the event loop during I/O operations (such as HTTP requests or database queries). If Service A reads a record, awaits an external API call, and then writes back an updated value, Service B can read the stale pre-update record during that exact window. items.title: 175 MB of Substrings to Read One Column
items.summary: I had a boring little job: a pile of CSV-shaped lines in memory, and I needed one number out of each — the amount column, third field, that's it. The rest of the row was along for the ride. I wrote the obvious loop, it gave the right total, and I moved on. Then the allocation profiler lit up on that exact loop and I went back to look. A million rows in, and I'd minted somewhere north of a hundred megabytes of garbage to read a single integer per line. Every other field I split out, I threw straight away. Here's the loop that did it: long total = 0; foreach (string line in lines) { string[] fields = line.Split(','); total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture); } line.Split(',') is doing precisely what I asked and nothing I wanted. For each row it allocates a string[] to hold the pieces, then allocates a fresh string for every field it finds, four of them on my data, copying the characters out of the original line into each one. I read fields[2] and let the array and the other three strings fall on the floor. Four columns, five allocations a row, one of them actually used. items.title: Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
items.summary: The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report: "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales. "Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. items.title: What it takes to turn an iPhone microphone into a decibel meter
items.summary: I work on Noise Meter at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that shows the sound level in decibels and logs a whole night of it, so someone with a noisy neighbour can show when it was loud. This post is about the measuring part: what happens between the microphone and the number on screen, and the places where I had to be honest about what a phone can't do. iOS processes microphone input by default: automatic gain, noise suppression, EQ. All of that is exactly what a meter must not have, because a quiet room would be boosted and a loud one pulled down. The audio session mode that turns it off is .measurement: try session.setCategory(.record, mode: .measurement) try session.setPreferredSampleRate(48_000) From there it is an AVAudioEngine input tap with a 4800-frame buffer, which is 100 ms at 48 kHz. I ask for 48 kHz but build the analyzer for whatever rate the hardware returns. I also select the built-in microphone's bottom data source with an omnidirectional pattern, and re-select it on every route change, because a route change can move the input. items.summary: If you've ever typed "build me an e-commerce app" into an AI tool, you know how it goes. You get something that runs, but it's not what you pictured. The login works differently than you wanted, the checkout has steps you never asked for, and half the buttons look like they came from different apps. The problem isn't the AI. It's that you left it hundreds of decisions to guess at. What worked for me was changing the order of things. I stopped asking for code first. Instead I ask Claude to help me write five short documents, answer its questions, and only then hand everything to Claude Code to build. The code ends up being the easy part. items.title: I built an iOS app where your documents delete themselves
items.summary: We keep too many documents forever. Scans of contracts, tickets, IDs sent for a one-time procedure, a rental agreement from three years ago. Most of them only matter for a short time, and then they just sit in your phone, your cloud and your photo library, waiting to be leaked, lost or forgotten. So I built Fadely: an iOS app that works as a vault for temporary documents. You add a document, choose a date, and when that date arrives the document destroys itself. My brother-in-law flies constantly. His passport was buried among hundreds of downloads on his phone, and he always worried: what if it gets stolen? So in Fadely, docs get an expiry date. Then they're gone for good. 🔒 Most storage apps are built on one assumption: keep everything, forever. Fadely does the opposite. Every document has an expiry date from the moment you save it. You decide how long it should exist, and the app takes care of the rest. items.title: What It Takes to Put Tab Autocomplete Inside Other Apps' Text Fields on macOS
items.summary: Autocomplete inside your own text view is a solved problem. You own the NSTextView, you know where the caret is, and you decide what Tab does. Autocomplete inside someone else's text field, in an app you did not write, is a different job. You don't own the text, the caret, or the Tab key. You borrow all three through macOS Accessibility, and each app lends them a little differently. We build DraftKey, a Mac app that suggests the rest of your sentence as you type and adds it when you press Tab. This post is about the plumbing behind that kind of feature. For the general mechanics I'm citing Apple's public documentation. For what we actually ran into, I'm citing our own public release notes: 52 tagged releases on GitHub, from 0.1.1 on September 20 to 0.1.62 on November 11, 2026. When I'm describing the macOS API surface in general rather than DraftKey's code, I'll say so. A Mac app can't read another app's text fields by default. items.title: Talking to an IBM i (AS/400) from .NET: data queues, COBOL and a live web page
items.summary: If you have ever heard "AS/400" and thought "that thing from the 80s", this article is for you. IBM i (the modern name of the AS/400) is still running payroll, banking and logistics in thousands of companies. Sooner or later, a .NET developer is asked to talk to it. By the end of this article you will know how to: get a free IBM i account and look around it; create a data queue (the IBM i message queue) and read it from .NET; call a COBOL program from C# and get its answer back; let that COBOL program publish a message that your .NET service consumes; see the whole thing in a small web page. Everything below was run for real against a free server. The code is a small open-source library plus a demo web app. IBM i / AS/400: a server with its own operating system. Same machine family, different names over the years. Library: roughly a schema or a folder. Objects live inside libraries (MYLIB/MYQUEUE). 5250 / green screen: the text terminal used to work on an IBM i. Data queue (*DTAQ): a message queue built into the system. items.summary: Reuters reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a third woman (source paywalled; alternative source ), an unnamed Nvidia employee. The revelation follows reports of two other extramarital affairs: one with Nvidia VP Kimberly Powell and another with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects of being a Chinese spy. The latter relationship has also prompted a shareholder lawsuit alleging Nvidia misled investors about its ties to a company suspected of circumventing U.S. chip export restrictions. Jensen Huang has since resigned as Nvidia's CEO and stepped down from its board on Thursday. CFO Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Four lessons from building a handwriting notes app for iPad
items.summary: I've been building GraphNotes, a notes app for iPad, iPhone Duo, and Mac where handwriting, PDF highlights and typed notes share one library. Two rules shaped most of its technical decisions: The ink is the note. The app reads your handwriting so it can search it, but it never swaps your strokes for its guess at what they say. Every thought keeps its way back. A note written beside a highlighted passage stays linked to that exact passage, and links point at permanent IDs, never at titles. It's built with SwiftUI (and UIKit where touch handling needs it), PencilKit, SQLite (libSQL through a fork of GRDB) and CloudKit's CKSyncEngine. Here are four things that took me longer to get right than I expected, in case they save you some time. It's tempting to spot new strokes by comparing drawing.strokes.count. Undo, redo and the vector eraser all break that. What works is diffing the strokes of two states by PKStrokePath.creationDate, the wall-clock time the pen touched down. items.summary: Google is launching its first Gemini-powered smart glasses, with Samsung supplying the computing hardware. Given their built-in 12-megapixel camera, Google is emphasizing privacy protections, including a tamper-resistant recording light, automatic face redaction, and restrictions on real-time facial recognition and livestreaming. The company also promises not to use captured photos or videos for AI training or targeted advertising. Ars Technica reports: Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses. The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we've seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. items.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
items.summary: A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code and potentially take control of affected server processes. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, the vulnerability affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled and is fixed in version 2.4.71. The Hacker News reports: The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported. HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host. items.title: F# for Beginners: Functional Programming on .NET
items.summary: F# is a functional-first language on .NET, made by Microsoft. If you know C#, you already know the ecosystem — the same libraries, the same runtime, the same tooling. What F# changes is how you write: less boilerplate, immutable data by default, and a type system that catches mistakes before your code runs. Many developers who try F# say their C# gets better afterwards, even if they never switch. A small example shows the difference: // average a list of numbers, safely let average numbers = match numbers with | [] -> None | xs -> Some (List.sum xs / float xs.Length) average [10.0; 20.0; 30.0] // Some 20.0 The Option type (Some or None) replaces null. Instead of a null reference crashing your program at runtime, the compiler forces you to handle the empty case. Pattern matching, pipelines (|>) and type inference mean F# programs are often half the length of the equivalent C# — and easier to read once you learn the idioms. F# is a good fit for backend services, data analysis, finance, and anywhere correctness matters. It is used in production for trading systems, web APIs (with Giraffe or Saturn), and data work. items.title: My Mac windows kept landing on the wrong Space after every monitor swap, so I wrote a small app for it
items.summary: I use a MacBook with one external monitor at a time, and I swap between a few monitors during the week. Every time I plug a monitor back in, macOS brings the windows back to that screen, but not to the Space they were on. Chrome ends up on desktop 3, Slack on desktop 1, and I spend the first few minutes dragging things around. I wanted something that remembers, for each monitor, which Space every window belongs to. I couldn't find a tool that did exactly that, so I wrote LayoutKeeper, a small menu bar app. What it does: Saves a window layout per external monitor, keyed by the monitor's EDID, including which Space each window is on. When that monitor is plugged back in, it moves windows back to their saved Space and position. Tells Chrome windows apart by profile, so work and personal windows go back to the right places. Adds brightness keys for external monitors. What it doesn't do yet: when you unplug and go back to the built-in screen only, it doesn't restore a separate layout for that. There is an open issue for it (#2) and it's the next thing I want to build. It's free and open source (GPL-3.0), with builds for Apple Silicon and Intel: https://github.com/tumingke0/LayoutKeeper

items.title: Building a Private Classifier with Apple's On-Device Model and NLContextualEmbedding
items.summary: Apple's on-device model is a small language model that ships with macOS and iOS. It runs offline, costs nothing per call, and never sends your data anywhere. This article covers what it is good at, where it falls short, and how to build a classification engine from two pieces: NLContextualEmbedding and the Foundation Models framework. Size and context. The model has roughly 3 billion parameters. Its context window was about 4,096 tokens at launch, and that budget covers instructions, prompt and response together. Check the context size on your target OS version, because it can change between releases. A long document will not fit, so plan to chunk it. Speed. It runs on the Neural Engine and GPU, and generation is fast enough to feel interactive on Apple silicon. Time to first token is short, so short classification calls come back quickly. Throughput varies a lot with the chip and with the length of the output, so measure on your own hardware before quoting numbers. What it is good for: Classifying and tagging text. items.title: Tim Peters, Python User #2 and Prolific Contributor, Dies At 74
items.summary: Tim Peters, one of Python's earliest and most influential contributors, died on July 15 at age 74. Known as Python's second real user, Peters created the Zen of Python and Timsort sorting algorithm while contributing to numerous core components. He also served as a Python Software Foundation director from 2001 to 2014. Adafruit remembers Peters in a blog post: He's best known for the Zen of Python, PEP 20, still printed by typing import this. In 2002, he gave Python Timsort, the sorting algorithm he designed for lists, later adopted by Java and Android. He also polished the cyclic garbage collector and the pymalloc allocator, worked on the dict implementation, the float object, the math module and Karatsuba multiplication in longobject, and wrote the first version of doctest, plus difflib, pickletools and tabnanny. He was a director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014. Before Python, he wrote compilers at Cray Research and speech-to-text software at Dragon Systems. The thread is full of recollections from core developers about his patient, detailed answers on the mailing lists, signed with his trademark . items.title: Power Grids On 5 Continents Pulse Every 60s. Scientists Think They Know Why
items.summary: "ScienceAlert is reporting that researchers may have finally determined why, for many years, power grids around the world have been pulsing every 60 seconds," writes longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot. The likely culprit? Uninterruptible power supplies running routine battery checks. From the report: Every minute, some uninterruptible power supplies perform routine battery checks, creating small but measurable surges in electricity demand. And it's like clockwork. "Even benign control routines can become systemically relevant when many devices act coherently," writes a team led by physicist Dirk Witthaut of the University of Cologne, Germany, in a paper published in Nature Energy. "Unintended synchronization can generate recurrent and potentially amplified oscillatory behavior in large-scale cyber-physical energy systems." To figure it out, Witthaut and his colleagues analyzed high-resolution electricity measurements from buildings at the Forschungszentrum Julich research campus in Germany. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from PBS: The historic ocean liner SS United States will be intentionally sunk Wednesday off the coast of the Florida panhandle. Live coverage of the sinking of the SS United States is expected to start at 1 p.m. EST, with the sinking expected at 2 p.m. EST. Watch live in the video player above. In its heyday, the SS United States crushed the trans-Atlantic speed record, which it still holds. The luxury ocean liner took only three days to cross from New York to Europe on its maiden voyage in 1952. Carrying presidents and Hollywood stars, the nearly 1,000-foot vessel was a technical marvel of its time. However, the rise of air travel and high operating costs sunk its economic viability, and the ship was pulled from service in 1969. The ocean liner sat at Philadelphia's Pier 82 for nearly 30 years. After a contentious back and forth with a pier landlord over rent and docking fees, Okaloosa County in Florida eventually stepped in to purchase the ship and bring it to the Gulf of Mexico to become the world's largest artificial reef. items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
items.summary: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.
